issues.legal_issue: A charge created by agreement and embodied in a registered compromise decree is a charge within the statutory law governing charges.
material_facts: The parties settled a money suit by compromise decree, and their agreement charged three items of immovable property to secure payment of the debt.
issues.conclusion: The charge created by the agreement embodied in the compromise decree was covered by the statutory provisions governing charges and constituted security created by act of the parties.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, a charge arises where immovable property is made security for payment of money without the transaction amounting to a mortgage. A compromise decree records the parties’ agreement rather than a judicial determination; when the agreement creates a charge and is duly registered, it creates security by act of the parties. The Court relied on Pulavarthi Venkata Subba Rao v. Valluri Jagannadha Rao for the character of a compromise decree.

rule.if: competing_priority_case and (property_made_security_for_debt by_party_agreement) and compromise_decree_records_agreement and decree_registered

predicates.competing_priority_case: The proceeding concerns competing claims to priority between a charge and a later interest in the same property.
predicates.property_made_security_for_debt: The property was made security for payment of a debt.
predicates.by_party_agreement: The security was created by an agreement of the parties rather than solely by a court's decision.
predicates.compromise_decree_records_agreement: The court embodied the parties’ agreement in a compromise decree.
predicates.decree_registered: The decree creating the charge was registered.

issues.definition: When parties agree to secure a debt against property, embody that agreement in a registered compromise decree, and the dispute concerns competing priorities, the decree creates a charge within the law governing charges.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory protection against enforcement of a charge against property transferred for consideration without notice does not extend to a simple mortgage.
material_facts: A prior charge had been created over the property by a compromise decree.
The property was later made subject to simple mortgages, under which the mortgagor retained possession.
The mortgagee had no actual or constructive notice of the charge.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the proviso to section 100 did not apply to mortgages, including simple mortgages; Beg J dissented and considered a simple mortgagee protected by the proviso.
issues.legal_principle: The majority construed the words “transferred for consideration” and “in the hands of” in the proviso to section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act as describing a transfer of the property, rather than the transfer of a limited interest such as a mortgage. It relied on the Act’s distinctions among transfer of property, transfer of an interest, sale, mortgage, and lease, including sections 5, 6, 8, 54, 58, 100, and 105. It distinguished English statutory meanings of “purchaser” and referred to Arumilli Surayya v. Pinisetti Venkataramanamma, while rejecting that case’s observation on this point as controlling. Beg J’s separate opinion read the proviso more broadly and disagreed.

rule.if: competing_priority_case and prior_charge_exists and simple_mortgage_created and mortgagee_acquired_limited_property_interest

predicates.competing_priority_case: The proceeding concerns competing priority claims involving a charge and a later interest in the same property.
predicates.prior_charge_exists: A charge over the property existed before the later transaction.
predicates.simple_mortgage_created: The later transaction created a simple mortgage without transferring possession of the property.
predicates.mortgagee_acquired_limited_property_inte: The mortgagee acquired a limited interest in the property rather than the transferor’s full ownership.

issues.definition: When a priority dispute involves an existing charge and a later simple mortgage that transfers only a limited interest, the simple mortgagee is not within the statutory proviso protecting a transferee of the property.

issues.legal_issue: Constructive notice of a registered transaction is not imputed when the transaction’s particulars are not correctly entered in the relevant registration index, and a reasonably diligent mortgagee had no actual notice.
material_facts: The decree was registered and noted in Book No. 1, but the property subject to the dispute was omitted from the relevant property index through an error in the Registrar’s office.
The property cards, municipal records, and indices did not disclose the charge.
The mortgagee had searched the registration records, and even a careful inquiry would not have disclosed the charge.
The courts below found that the mortgagee had neither actual nor constructive notice.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the mortgagee had no actual or constructive notice of the charge was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3, Explanation I, of the Transfer of Property Act, including its proviso, requires registration to be completed as prescribed, the instrument to be duly entered or filed in the books required by section 51 of the Registration Act, and the transaction particulars to be correctly entered in the indices required by section 55. Because the property particulars were omitted from the relevant index, constructive notice could not be imputed. The Court also applied section 3’s general rule concerning actual knowledge, wilful abstention from inquiry, and gross negligence.

rule.if: mortgage_priority_dispute and registered_instrument_exists and relevant_property_index_omits_transaction and actual_notice_absent and reasonable_search_made

predicates.mortgage_priority_dispute: The proceeding concerns the priority of a mortgagee against a prior charge.
predicates.registered_instrument_exists: An instrument recording the prior transaction was registered.
predicates.relevant_property_index_omits_transactio: The index used to identify transactions affecting the property omitted the transaction or its relevant particulars.
predicates.actual_notice_absent: The later mortgagee did not actually know of the prior charge.
predicates.reasonable_search_made: The later mortgagee made the kind of search reasonably expected of a prudent person, and that search would not have revealed the charge.

issues.definition: In a mortgage priority dispute, a registered instrument does not give the mortgagee constructive notice if the relevant property index omits the transaction, and a mortgagee who lacked actual notice made a reasonable search.

issues.legal_issue: A later mortgagee with notice of a prior charge takes subject to that charge, while a mortgagee without notice has priority over the charge under the equitable notice principle.
material_facts: The compromise decree created an earlier charge over the property.
The later mortgagee had no actual or constructive notice because the relevant property index and other searched records did not disclose the charge.
The property was later sold in execution of the decree, and the mortgagee sought to recover the mortgage debt.
issues.conclusion: Although the majority held that the proviso to section 100 did not apply to mortgages, it concluded that the later mortgage had priority because the mortgagee lacked notice of the prior charge; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The majority applied the doctrine of notice as an equitable principle administered in accordance with justice, equity, and good conscience: a subsequent mortgagee with notice of a prior charge takes subject to it, but a mortgagee without notice has priority over the charge. The Court discussed section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, section 48 of the Registration Act, and section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 (corresponding to section 19(b) of the 1963 Act), and referred to Nemai Charan v. Kokil Bag and Chhaganlal v. Chunnilal. It held that this equitable result did not justify changing the meaning of section 100.

rule.if: competing_priority_case and prior_charge_exists and later_mortgage_exists and mortgagee_lacks_notice

predicates.competing_priority_case: The proceeding concerns competing priority claims between an earlier charge and a later mortgage over the same property.
predicates.prior_charge_exists: A charge over the property existed before the mortgage.
predicates.later_mortgage_exists: A mortgage over the property was created after the charge.
predicates.mortgagee_lacks_notice: The later mortgagee had neither actual nor constructive notice of the earlier charge.

issues.definition: When a later mortgagee has no notice of an earlier charge in a dispute over the same property, the mortgage has priority over the charge.

issues.legal_issue: The priority dispute between a charge and a later mortgage is not determined by the statutory rule for competing transfers of interests in property.
material_facts: The earlier right was a charge created by a compromise decree, not a transfer of an interest in the property.
The later transaction was a simple mortgage, which transferred an interest in the property.
The competing claims concerned priority against the same property.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act did not determine the priority between the charge and the mortgage; the applicable analysis was governed by the law of charges and notice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act addresses rights created by transfers at different times and requires competing rights that cannot coexist or be exercised to their full extent. A charge is not a transfer of an interest in property, so the section does not itself resolve priority between a charge and a mortgage. The Court considered sections 48 and 100 of the Act.

rule.if: competing_priority_case and prior_charge_exists and later_mortgage_exists and charge_is_not_transfer_of_property_interest

predicates.competing_priority_case: The proceeding concerns priority between an earlier charge and a later mortgage over the same property.
predicates.prior_charge_exists: A charge over the property existed before the mortgage.
predicates.later_mortgage_exists: A mortgage over the property was created after the charge.
predicates.charge_is_not_transfer_of_property_inter: The earlier charge created security but did not transfer an interest in the property.

issues.definition: When an earlier charge is not a transfer of an interest in property, the statutory priority rule for competing transfers does not determine its priority against a later mortgage.

issues.legal_issue: The doctrine of lis pendens does not apply when the property was not directly and specifically in issue in the pending suit and no execution proceeding was pending when the later mortgage was created.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought recovery of a money debt, and the property was not directly and specifically in issue in that suit.
The charge over the property was created by agreement in the compromise decree.
No execution application was pending when the mortgages were created.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of lis pendens did not apply to the later mortgages.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act requires, among other things, a pending non-collusive suit or proceeding in which rights to the immovable property are directly and specifically in question. The Court agreed that the later mortgages were not affected because the property was not the subject matter of the original money suit and no execution proceeding was pending when they were created.

predicates.lis_pendens_issue: The proceeding raises whether a later transfer is affected by the doctrine governing dealings with property during litigation.
predicates.property_not_directly_in_issue_in_pendin: The pending suit did not directly and specifically put rights to the property in issue.
predicates.no_execution_pending_when_later_mortgage: No execution proceeding concerning the decree was pending when the later mortgage was created.

issues.definition: When litigation does not directly and specifically place the property in issue and no execution proceeding is pending at the time of the later mortgage, the doctrine of lis pendens does not apply.
